blocks.text: A2 Demand model

The demand model takes international arrivals from 1,498,829 in 2025 to 1,822,634, 2,175,778 or 2,516,282 in 2035, and its base case crosses the 1.8 million seat line the model draws, at the 2030 year point.
Method

The model sets a growth rate for each source market from four levers and projects arrivals from the base year to 2035 (Demand-Side Analysis, Jun 2026, p18, p20). The levers are source market growth, Western Cape penetration of source-market outbound, an airlift capacity ceiling and structural market conditions. Source-market growth sets the ceiling: "WC cannot sustainably grow faster than it's source market is generating travellers" (Demand-Side Analysis, Jun 2026, p18). Projections are anchored on OAG aviation data and Skift global traveller data (Demand-Side Analysis, Jun 2026, p8).
Scenario definitions

The three scenarios vary intervention, not demand: "The difference between scenarios is not demand potential, but the extent to which structural barriers are removed and growth opportunities are actively pursued" (Demand-Side Analysis, Jun 2026, p19).

Base-case spend

blocks.caption: Base-case spend by group
blocks.source: Market Assessment Report, May 2026, p24 (working analysis; comma decimals on the slide shown here as points). Values in R billion. Change is computed. The 2030 group cells sum to 33.72 against the printed 33.71 total, a rounding difference (computed).
blocks.message: At fixed average spend per group, base-case tourism spend rises from a modelled R27.12bn in 2024 to R40.59bn in 2035.

blocks.text: The 2030 and 2035 values equal each group's arrivals times its average spend, so spend per arrival within a group stays fixed (computed). Dividing the 2024 values by the same assumptions implies 1,445,116 arrivals, close to the June base of 1,445,031 (computed). The slide calls the 2024 values modelled, and the same deck reports foreign direct spend of R22.7bn in FY2024 (Market Assessment Report, May 2026, p10, p24). The June deck prints no spend projection.
Seat line and model limits

Both decks state that "Current air access places a hard ceiling at 1.8 million inbound seats, meaning the projected growth cannot be realised without additional capacity or frequency" (Market Assessment Report, May 2026, p20; Demand-Side Analysis, Jun 2026, p21). Neither deck prints the seats behind the line or a load factor that converts seats into arrivals. At the 79% average load factor, 1.8 million seats would carry about 1.42 million arrivals, below the 1.57 million recorded in FY25/26, so this report reads the line as the model's assumption, not a measured cap (section 1.3).

The model prints its seat line and six base-case year points but no seat table, annual series or group split for the other scenarios. The seat line is 1.8 million inbound seats, drawn as a line labelled 1.8M and called current, with no year or seat definition (Market Assessment Report, May 2026, p20; Demand-Side Analysis, Jun 2026, p21). Neither deck states the year the line is crossed: 2028 (1,673,855) sits below the line and 2030 (1,802,929) is the first point above it (Market Assessment Report, May 2026, p20; Demand-Side Analysis, Jun 2026, p21).

No seat table is printed: there are no seats by route or year, no load factors and no frequencies (Market Assessment Report, May 2026, p17, p20; Demand-Side Analysis, Jun 2026, p18). Nor is an annual series: 2026, 2027, 2029, 2031 and 2033 are absent, and the June chart starts at 2024, not 2025 (Market Assessment Report, May 2026, p20; Demand-Side Analysis, Jun 2026, p21). The conservative and accelerated scenarios appear at 2035 only, with no group split, no year points and no per-market rates (Market Assessment Report, May 2026, p19; Demand-Side Analysis, Jun 2026, p20).

The calendar or financial basis and the source series of the 1,498,829 base are not stated, and the 2025 bars are not marked as actuals or model values (Market Assessment Report, May 2026, p19, p20; Demand-Side Analysis, Jun 2026, p22 to p25). ACSA passenger arrivals (1.57m in FY25/26), SAT tourist arrivals, OAG air arrivals and model arrivals are not reconciled (Demand-Side Analysis, Jun 2026, p8, p11, p13, p20, p27).
